source.title: Buddhist response to the crystal argument: cognition is inherently self-manifesting (svaprakāśa/svasaṃvitti)
source.author: Dharmakīrti, Dignāga, Ñāṇavīra Thera

external_sources.title: Consciousness and Causality: Dharmakīrti Against Physicalism
external_sources.author: Christian Coseru

source_span.locator: Pramāṇavārttika 3, cited in Coseru — Dignāga's PS(V) 1.9ab
source_span.quote: Cognition arises actually with two appearances, self-appearance and object-appearance. The self-awareness of this cognition possessing both appearances is the result.

claims.claim_text: The Buddhist epistemological tradition (Dignāga, Dharmakīrti) does NOT claim that determination-by-exclusion alone accounts for consciousness. Rather, every cognition has two appearances: self-appearance (svābhāsa) and object-appearance (viṣayābhāsa). Self-awareness (svasaṃvitti) is the result — cognition is inherently self-manifesting. The crystal argument misfires because it assumes the Buddhist position lacks an account of sentience, when in fact svasaṃvitti (self-awareness of cognition) is a core doctrine of the tradition.
claims.hetu: Dignāga and Dharmakīrti explicitly argue every cognition has self-appearance
claims.sadhya: the Buddhist tradition has an account of self-awareness distinct from determination-by-exclusion
claims.vyapti_statement: If cognition has two appearances (self and object), then self-awareness is intrinsic to cognition, not an added extra.

falsifier.condition: Show that the Buddhist svasaṃvitti doctrine reduces to determination-by-exclusion with no remainder — i.e., that self-appearance is identical to object-appearance in the Buddhist account.

claims.reasoning: Direct textual evidence from Dignāga's PS(V) 1.9ab, the foundational text of Buddhist epistemology. Cognition has two distinct appearances — self and object. Self-awareness is not reducible to determination-by-exclusion.

source_span.locator: Notes on Dhamma — Viññāṇa, §d on reflexive presence
source_span.quote: In reflexion, different degrees of consciousness, of presence, will be apparent. Distinction should be made between immediate presence and reflexive presence.

claims.claim_text: Nanavira's account: consciousness (viññāṇa) is the presence of a phenomenon, and that presence is reflexively given. 'There is eye-consciousness — eye-consciousness is present reflexively.' Consciousness is not an entity that needs an extra property to be sentient. It is the presence-of-phenomena, and presence as such is inherently reflexive. The crystal argument assumes consciousness is a 'thing' that requires vimarśa to be sentient, but for Nanavira, reflexivity is not an added property — it is how presence works structurally.
claims.hetu: consciousness is presence-of-phenomena, not a thing; reflexivity is structural
claims.sadhya: the crystal argument assumes a substantive view of consciousness that Nanavira's framework does not hold
claims.vyapti_statement: If consciousness IS presence rather than a thing, then the question 'does structure produce sentience?' is misapplied — presence as such is already reflexive.

falsifier.condition: Show that Nanavira's account of reflexive presence reduces to mere structural determination without sentience — i.e., that 'presence reflexively given' is compatible with insentience.

claims.reasoning: Nanavira's Viññāṇa note directly addresses the nature of consciousness as presence. The immediate/reflexive presence distinction shows reflexivity is structural, not an added property.

source_span.locator: Coseru — Jitāri's proof of cognition's self-manifestation
source_span.quote: all things that become manifest in consciousness are cognition, which has the nature of self-manifestation

claims.claim_text: The combined Buddhist response to Abhinavagupta's crystal argument: (1) The Dharmakīrti tradition holds that cognition is inherently self-manifesting (svaprakāśa) via svasaṃvitti — it does not need an external vimarśa to be sentient. (2) Nanavira's framework treats consciousness as structurally reflexive presence — sentience is built into the structure of presence, not added by a separate property. (3) The crystal argument assumes a substantive metaphysics of consciousness as a 'thing' that needs an extra quality. Neither the Dharmakīrti nor the Nanavira framework holds this view. The critique misfires.
claims.hetu: both traditions have accounts of self-awareness distinct from determination-by-exclusion
claims.sadhya: the crystal argument does not apply to the Buddhist position as actually held
claims.vyapti_statement: If a critique assumes a metaphysics that the target does not hold, the critique misfires regardless of its internal validity.

falsifier.condition: Show that Abhinavagupta's crystal argument was specifically directed at a svasaṃvitti-style account and remains effective against it — i.e., that the Tantrāloka passage explicitly considers and refutes the Buddhist self-awareness doctrine.

claims.reasoning: Synthetic claim combining both Buddhist responses. The falsifier is important: if Abhinavagupta already considered svasaṃvitti and rejected it in the crystal argument, the Buddhist response needs a different tack.
